steps.action:
The first storm of the season rolled in before dawn, and with it came the sound that Daniel Hale dreaded most: silence.

Not the silence of calm seas or sleeping gulls, but the hollow, wrong kind of silence—the kind left behind when something that has always been there suddenly isn’t. It slid in between the gusts of wind and under the booming of waves tearing at the cliff, a silence shaped exactly like a missing light.

He felt it rather than heard it, standing at his kitchen window with a chipped mug cradled in his hands. The glass rattled in the frame as a rogue gust slammed into the side of the stone tower. Rain smeared the dawn into an indistinct gray. He watched the horizon—habit, more than hope—and squinted toward where the light should have been painting its long white arc across the water.

Nothing.

The Farfast Point beacon had gone dark.

Daniel set the mug in the sink and hurried through the narrow hallway to the spiral staircase, his boots thudding on the old, uneven boards. The tower smelled of oil and salt and old paint, and the stone walls sweated with damp. As he climbed, the familiar ache lit up in his right knee, a deep, grinding complaint from an injury twenty years healed and never forgiven. He took the steps two at a time anyway.

This lighthouse had been his world for thirty-two years. Longer than his marriage had lasted, longer than his youth, longer even than some of the wrecks they said the light had saved. Every crack in the stairs, every quirk of the wiring, every stubborn bolt in the lantern room belonged to his memory: a private, cataloged universe atop a jagged strip of rock.

He reached the service deck just beneath the lantern room and stopped, leaning one hand against the cold iron railing as he caught his breath. Wind howled at the tower’s glass top, a constant roar broken only by the occasional sharp whistle of a higher gust. Lightning flickered faintly beyond the storm’s edge, far offshore, impatient.

He turned the last bend of the stair and shouldered open the heavy door to the lantern room.

It was darker than it should have been. The world beyond the glass was a smeared watercolor—gray sky, darker gray sea, white streaks of foam clawing at the cliffs—but inside, the great Fresnel lens sat like a glass cathedral, motionless and dull.

Daniel’s chest tightened in an old, familiar way. Lights went out. Bulbs burned through. Fuses gave up. In thirty-two years he had responded with calm, methodical competence. But the storm was early, the sea was bad, and the main shipping lane cut within five miles of Farfast Point. Out there, captains would be trusting this light to burn where their charts said it would be: A steady white, twenty seconds, visible for seventeen nautical miles.

He crossed the metal floor and checked the control panel first. The digital display flickered weakly, then cut out entirely as another roll of thunder shook the glass. The panel’s status lights—normally a reassuring little row of greens—were dead.

He flipped the main breaker off, waited, turned it on again. No response.

A surge, he thought. Or the old transformer finally gave up the ghost.

He opened the maintenance cabinet and pulled out the toolkit by feel. The storm made the room dim enough that he could see his own breath against the glass; the heating elements hadn’t cycled on, which meant they weren’t getting power either. He unlatched the metal cover on the electrical box and peered in.

A blackened streak cut across the back plate, fanning out from the surge protection relay. One of the main lines had fried, vaporizing a small section of insulation and leaving a scorch mark that stank faintly of burned plastic even through the salt-damp air.

He exhaled slowly through his teeth.

“Well,” he said aloud, his voice swallowed by the wind. “You picked your moment.”

He should have replaced that relay last year when it first started acting finicky. Budget requests for the station had been redirected—automated systems were the future, the email had said—and there was always just enough life left in the old equipment to justify putting it off. He’d worked around it. He’d gotten used to coaxing the failing parts along, like an old sailor sweet-talking a stubborn engine.

But the sea didn’t care about budgets and modernization plans.

He pulled his radio from his shoulder and thumbed the transmit key. It crackled, half static.

“Farfast Station to Harbor Control, copy.”

Only the hiss of interference answered. Lightning picked that moment to flash closer, the afterimage painting pale bars across the inside of his eyelids.

The tower’s external antenna was as old as the wiring; if the surge had climbed high enough, it could have fried the repeater, too. Or the storm was just thick enough to choke the signal. On the tiny screen, the transmission icon blinked, valiantly optimistic, then dropped.

He clipped the radio back on and scrubbed a hand over his beard, short and salt-and-pepper and bristling.

If he couldn’t fix the grid feed, he’d have to run the auxiliary. And if the relay was truly dead, it meant bypassing safety systems he’d been trained never to touch. But there was a ship out there, surely more than one, with eyes on a horizon where no light waited.

Daniel tightened his jaw and went to fetch the emergency kit.

The auxiliary lamp waited in its steel case near the base of the lens assembly, exactly where regulation required it. Daniel knelt, knee complaining, and flipped the latches. Inside, the portable halogen array sat cradled in foam, bright orange casing dulled by years of dust and salt. He pulled it out carefully—it was heavy, ungainly—and worked it free of its cables.

The manual generator, a squat diesel thing that had once been painted a cheerful yellow, brooded in the corner like an annoyed toad. He checked the fuel gauge. Half a tank. Enough for several hours at least.

“If you start,” he muttered at it, “I’ll never complain about that noise again.”

The starter motor coughed once, twice, then caught reluctantly. The generator roared to life, rattling the lantern room floor. The sound was a comfort, a solid growl underneath the chaotic thunder. The overhead light flickered on for a moment, then off again as some overloaded relay tripped. The generator didn’t care; its power line was hardwired solely to the emergency array.

He hoisted the lamp, grunting as the weight pulled at his shoulder, and lugged it to the outer ring where the main lens sat. Mounting brackets were built for just this scenario. He locked the array into place just beneath the Fresnel lens, lined it up roughly with the seaward arc, and connected the thick power cable from the generator. Then he flipped the switch.

Nothing.

He frowned and checked the inline breaker. It was on. Connections secure. He toggled the lamp’s power again. Still nothing.

He popped open the back plate on the lamp with the edge of his screwdriver, fingers moving more from muscle memory than conscious thought. Inside, the night’s real culprit revealed itself: corrosion around the primary contact, a salty green crust that crumbled under his thumb. Years of damp, condensed breath, and not enough maintenance budgets.

He could clean it. He had sandpaper, contact cleaner. But the minutes were pouring away like water over the cliff. Anything could be out in that gray soup—a lone fishing trawler running late, the mail boat from Harrow Bay cutting across the point to shave half an hour, an out-of-town captain who trusted his GPS more than a chart.

Or some tourist yacht, he thought unkindly, following a blinking line on their phone.

For all his frustrations with the world beyond the tower, Daniel understood this much: ships steered by expectation as much as by instruments. Even the most careful mariner felt easier when a lighthouse burned where it should.

He glanced at the brass clock bolted to the wall. 5:42 a.m. Civil dawn, on a clear day. In this storm, dawn meant only that the black turned to charcoal. Sunrise was still nearly an hour away, and even then the cloud cover would keep the sea dim.

He worked quickly, scraping away corrosion, spraying cleaner, rubbing the contact points until they shone like dull silver. His fingers went numb from cold and effort, but when he finished and closed the back up again, his breath had steadied.

He flipped the switch once more.

The lamp thumped, hummed, then flared to life with a harsh blue-white brilliance that seemed to shove the dimness back in a circle around the tower. The Fresnel lens caught the light eagerly, breaking it, bending it, gathering it into a focused beam that seared out into the storm.

He heard it more than saw it, the way the sudden presence of the beam pushed back that terrible absence. The silence of missing light retreated, filled by a soundless shout that pulsed with each slow sweep of the lens. The automated rotation motor, at least, still functioned; the beam moved, methodically carving the horizon.

Daniel exhaled and leaned his forehead against the cool glass.

“There you are,” he whispered. “There you are.”

He stayed there, watching the beam, counting the seconds of its circuit. Twenty, as it should be. Steady and faithful.

For a few minutes he allowed himself to simply stand, to feel the storm rattling around him and the tower answering with its patient, immovable weight. The sea hurled itself at the cliffs, again and again, as it had for centuries. The lighthouse did what it had always done: it stood, and it shone.

His radio crackled.

“—ast Station, this is Harbor Control. Farfast, do you copy?”

He tugged the device free and thumbed the key. “Farfast here. Took you long enough.”

“We’re reading you now,” the voice came back, threaded with both relief and irritation. It was Mark Jensen, the current Harbor Control supervisor, a man thirty years his junior who wore his uniform crisp and his smile thin. “We lost your AIS ping and light signature about twenty minutes ago. Status?”

“Main grid feed’s out. Surge fried the internal relay. I’m running on auxiliary diesel with the portable lamp.” He glanced at the generator, listening to its steady chug. “It’s holding.”

“Copy. Any injuries?”

“No. Just older than I like to admit.”

There was a crackle that might have been a chuckle, or static.

“Be advised, the tanker Mistral Dawn altered course ten minutes ago, reported visual absence of your light, then regained a bearing on what they describe as a ‘weak but present beam.’ I assume that’s your emergency.”

“That’d be it,” Daniel said. “Weak?”

“Compared to your usual intensity, yes. But they have you.” Mark’s voice shifted, growing more formal as he consulted something on his end. “Coast Guard wants a full systems report once the storm passes. There’s talk of… expediting the automation upgrade for Farfast.”

That had been hovering over every conversation with headquarters for the past five years: automation. Remote oversight. Unmanned stations with sensors and solar arrays and cameras that could be monitored from an office two hundred miles away. No more lone keepers pacing towers in the dark, no more weather-beaten faces behind brass-rimmed binoculars.

No more Daniel.

“Of course there is,” he said quietly.

“Come again?”

“Copy. I’ll have your report,” he said, more crisply. “For now, I suggest advising eastbound traffic to keep at least seven miles offshore until further notice. This storm’s chewing up the inshore routes.”

“Acknowledged. Anything else you need?”

“Send someone with a new relay and some better contact cleaner when it’s safe. And coffee. The cheap stuff you people drink down there.”

This time the amused snort was definite. “Roger that, Farfast. Stay upright.”

The radio clicked off, leaving him alone with the drum of rain and the generator’s roar and the patient sweep of the light.

He stood a long while, watching the horizon in the intervals between flashes. Every now and then, a momentary gap in the leading edge of the storm showed him something—a white smudge of foam farther out, the black triangle of a distant ship’s bow cutting through the chop.

He tried not to think about what would have happened if the auxiliary hadn’t started. If the corrosion had been worse. If his hands had fumbled. He tried not to imagine the invisible shapes out there, the hulls sliding a little too close to the unseen teeth of rock that lurked beneath the surface.

The beam revolved. Twenty seconds. Twenty seconds. Twenty seconds.

He thought of the first time he’d climbed those stairs. He had been twenty-four, lean and impatient, his head full of half-formed plans about seeing the world from a deck instead of a cliff. His father’s old friend, Keeper Morgan, had watched him struggle up with two sacks of provisions and a toolbox and laughed.

“You think the sea is out there,” Morgan had said, jerking his chin toward the window slit that showed a thin strip of gray-blue. “Everyone does, at first. But she’s in here, too. In the stone, in the metal, in the way the light moves. Don’t let the loneliness spook you. It’s only her way of giving you room to listen.”

He hadn’t understood then. Now, decades later, with the skin at the corners of his eyes etched by sun and wind and ocean glare, he did.

The sea was never quiet. Even when the weather was calm, she muttered. Waves talked to rock, and rock answered back slowly, over years. Gulls marked the boundary between the high, bright sky and the heavy water with their cries. The wind translated things between them, in gusts and sighs.

In between all of that, there was the work of the light.

He had married on a calm July afternoon, in the little chapel in town. They’d strung netting and fairy lights, arranged driftwood along the aisle, filled jars with wildflowers. The guests had clapped and thrown dried petals when they walked out. He remembered the exact warmth of the sun on the back of his neck, the feel of his new wife’s hand in his.

By November, she’d told him she couldn’t live with the winter isolation, the constant worry when he stayed at the lighthouse through storms, the sense that he belonged more to this tower and the sea it served than to their kitchen and their bed. She deserved more than half a husband, she’d said, eyes bright and wet.

He’d stood on the cliff afterward, watching the beam sweep the black water, and felt something inside him catch on a jagged edge it never quite worked free of.

Just a little longer, he’d thought then. Another year. Two. Enough to train someone else, enough to feel like he was leaving this stone and steel in good hands.

Thirty-two years later, he was still promising the sea “just a little longer.”

Automation would make that promise for him, in a sense. The new systems would maintain the light’s schedule with indifferent perfection. Sensors would report malfunctions immediately. Redundancies would be triple-checked, all from the comfort of an office chair miles inland. No more delays when a breaker tripped. No more missed bulbs. No more old men with aching knees scrambling up iron stairs while storm winds tried to tear the world down.

It was right, he knew. Logical, safer, cost-effective—every argument lined up as neatly as buoys in a channel.

Still, watching the emergency beam struggle to cut through the storm’s gloom, he felt something like grief rising in his chest.

He stayed on duty through the full arc of the storm’s worst, checking the generator every half hour, listening to the pitch of its engine like a doctor at a patient’s bedside. He radioed Harbor Control twice more, gave updates on visibility and wind: dropping from gale to strong breeze, rain turning from hammer blows to a steady hiss.

By the time the first real slant of morning light found its way through thinning clouds, the emergency beam was a pale ghost against the gray. The sea had transformed from furious, churning slate to a sullen, rolling steel-blue, streaked with foam but no longer trying to climb the cliffs.

The edges of the world sharpened. He could see the far headland now, the faint pale line of surf breaking on the outer shoals. Somewhere out there, the Mistral Dawn and her steel bulk had steamed safely past, corrected for the brief absence of a light that had always been there.

Daniel shut down the generator. The sudden absence of its roar left his ears ringing. In that raw, echoing quiet, the sound of the waves felt almost gentle.

He looked at the dead control panel for the main array and patted it once, almost apologetically.

“They’ll fix you,” he said. “Better than I ever could.”

He made his way down the stairs slowly this time, each spiral of the tower revealing a familiar detail: the rust streak on the east-facing slit window, where condensation always gathered; the notch in the fifth step from the top, worn deeper by his own tread over years; the little shelf with the faded photograph of Keeper Morgan leaning against the railing, grinning into the wind.

In the kitchen at the base, he flicked the kettle on and listened to its small, domestic rumble. He poured himself fresh coffee—strong, dark—and stood by the window again, watching as the late morning brightened the day by increments.

The sea didn’t look benign, exactly. She never did. But she looked spent, rolling and breathing and rearranging herself after the fury.

He didn’t hear the boat until it was almost at the foot of the cliff. The small, thrumming engine cut through the dull roar of waves. He leaned closer to the window and saw the harbor launch nudging up to the bottom of the rusted metal stairs that clung to the rock face.

Two figures in orange jackets clambered out, one of them moving with the cautious care of someone not used to wet iron. The other bounded up the steps with easy balance. The wind off the receding storm tugged at their hoods.

He recognized Mark’s gait even at a distance.

By the time they knocked—three firm raps on the heavy oak door—Daniel had set two mugs on the table, laid out the tin of biscuits with its dented lid.

The younger technician with Mark had a tool case almost as big as he was and eyes that darted everywhere, taking in the interior of the tower hungrily. Fresh out of whatever academy churned out modern keepers-of-systems, Daniel guessed.

“Morning,” Mark said, stomping water off his boots. “We brought your relay. And coffee. Though I see you beat us to it.”

“This damned place would fall into the sea faster without coffee than without the light,” Daniel said. He glanced at the younger man. “You must be the fix-it wizard.”

“Corporal Elias Chen, Coast Guard Maintenance,” the lad said, flushing slightly. “It’s an honor, sir. I read the report about the Norwell trawler. The one you guided in during the ’09 blizzard.”

“That was more about them being too stubborn to stay in harbor than anything heroic on my part.” He poured coffee into the mugs and gestured to the chairs
